stances.claim: The Jan 6 Capitol attack was a heretofore-unthinkable assault on democracy and capitalism in the very temple where American liberalism is worshipped, practiced, and exported -- making it not merely a domestic incident but a global system threat.

Discontent morphs into insurrection when the rich-poor gap becomes unconscionably wide and is aggravated by ostentatious profligacy; populations then embrace populist demagogues like Trump, so the structural cause is inequality plus arrogance, not just political rhetoric.

Marx's wealth-redistribution answer has utterly failed -- the staunchest communists abandoned it, the Soviet Union collapsed, and even China rose only by adopting capitalism and private initiative; the answer is not to replace capitalism but to make it inclusive.

The international model is corporate inclusiveness -- Grameen Bank's collateral-free loans, Aravind Eye Hospital's universal cataract surgery, InfoGeekie's digital personalized learning -- proving inclusive capitalism is self-sustainable, not charity.

Filipino conglomerates and their foundations are already practicing the same inclusiveness -- Jollibee, BPI, CARD MRI, Metrobank Foundation, Lopez, Metro Pacific, PLDT, the conglo-stewarded universities, and San Miguel's P1B pandemic vaccine purchase -- making the inclusive-capitalism path locally credible.

The best way of governing is to govern the least, allow people their innovation and initiative, and interfere only to check avarice and level the playing field; government's primary role is to create just societies and improve access to basic necessities, encourage philanthropy, honor commitments, and protect property rights.

notable_anecdotes: The 'temple' framing of the US Capitol -- 'the very temple where the American brand of liberalism, freedom, and private initiative is worshipped, practiced, and exported' -- one of CJ's most intensely sacralized images of an American institution.

The catalog of profligacy markers -- 'private jets, luxury yachts, flamboyant sports cars, mansions galore, red diamonds' -- five rapid-fire concrete signifiers used as the explanatory cause of populist discontent.

The China observation -- capitalism and private initiative propelling it from poverty to 'second largest (and soon, the largest) economy in the world in barely three decades' -- used as the empirical refutation of Marx without ideological hostility.

The Yunus-Aravind-InfoGeekie triad ranked as international cases, paired against an extended Filipino enumeration (Jollibee, BPI, CARD MRI, Metrobank, Lopez, Metro Pacific, plus seven university/educational entries) -- the column's structural assertion that Philippine practice already matches global best practice.
The San Miguel P1B-for-70,000-employees vaccine line -- the single concrete pandemic-response figure in the column, presented as proof of conglomerate scale and seriousness.
The closing governance manifesto -- 'the best way of governing is to govern the least' -- a rare CJ articulation of his libertarian-leaning political philosophy in a single sentence.

one_paragraph_summary: Reading the Jan 6, 2021 Capitol riot as a 'heretofore unthinkable assault on democracy and capitalism' in the 'very temple' of American liberalism, Panganiban argues that discontent morphs into insurrection when the gap between rich and poor becomes unconscionably wide and is aggravated by an arrogant display of profligacy -- private jets, luxury yachts, sports cars, mansions, red diamonds -- pushing populations toward populist demagogues like Trump. Marx's redistribution answer has utterly failed; even China rose only by embracing capitalism. The path is therefore not replacement but inclusion. He cites three international examples -- Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank, India's Aravind Eye Hospital, and InfoGeekie -- and then enumerates Filipino counterparts: Jollibee's Farmer Entrepreneurship Program, BPI BanKo, Jaime Aristotle Alip's CARD MRI, Metrobank Foundation's Manila Doctors Hospital, Lopez Group's Green advocacies, Metro Pacific's GabayKabuhayan, and the conglomerate stewardship of UE (Tan Yan Kee), Mapua and U. Nueva Caceres (Yuchengco/Ayala), National University (SM), eight institutions under Phinma, and PLDT's GabayGuro for teachers. San Miguel's P1B vaccine commitment for 70,000 employees illustrates the pandemic response. He closes with a governance manifesto: 'the best way of governing is to govern the least,' interfering only to check avarice and level the playing field, while improving access to food, water, education, infrastructure, health care, and decent incomes -- liberal democracy and performance-driven capitalism remain the best catalysts for liberty and prosperity, but must scale up the inclusion of the poor and powerless.
